To overcome these limitations, we developed a novel efficient and generalized approach for federated learning that enables the reliable and accurate automated classification of TIL. This approach allows for the combination of data from diverse institutions and reduces the need for lyophilsized lymphocyte samples in training models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by comparing the performance of models trained via a federated method to those trained using more common techniques. The results show that our approach yields a mean AUC of 0.93 on the LymphNode19 challenge after only 5 rounds of federated training. The models produced also exhibit robust performance on unseen data, achieving a 0.02 increase in AUC when compared to similar studies. Traditional Poisson autoregressive models have been effective in analyzing such data, but they typically require the specification of fixed seasonal components. In contrast, a novel Temporally Varying Poisson Autoregressive (TVPAR) model is presented in this study, allowing the seasonal components to change over time. A maximum likelihood estimation approach is developed and proven to be consistent in estimating TVPAR parameters. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates the asymptotic normality of the estimated parameters, enabling the construction of a confidence interval for time-varying parameters. Through numerical simulations, the performance of maximum likelihood estimation is evaluated under different conditions, including large and medium-sized samples. The TVPAR model is applied to actual data sets, including counts of system crashes in a network and sales data, to illustrate its applicability and relevance. The findings indicate that the TVPAR model outperforms fixed seasonal PAR models in terms of prediction accuracy. The TVPAR model is an advancement over conventional Poisson autoregressive models, capable of handling complex, temporally varying patterns in time series data. For objects with distinct textures and colors, determining their pose is a well-defined problem. However, for objects with similar or mirror-like patterns, posing them poses a significant challenge. This difficulty significantly increases for rotating objects with pattern similarities, posing them even further. To tackle this problem, we propose an innovative two-stage approach called DeepHMap++ that learns from rotating objects with similar patterns. Initially, the framework identifies clusters through merged projection clustering, defining a pose-defined coordinate system. Next, correspondence learning stage uses this reference frame to pinpoint the object's pose by matching features in a pose-agnostic manner, ignoring pattern similarities. Unlike other pose estimation methods that rely on pose-specific training, our approach uses a pose-agnostic training method, ensuring accuracy even with rotating objects having similar patterns. DeepHMap++ is evaluated on a newly created dataset and compared to state-of-the-art clustering and pose estimation methods, demonstrating its superior performance. The implementation and testing of this approach are also open-sourced for review and examination. Additionally, we explore various features and parameters with which the approach can be implemented, in addition to making the paper's source code freely available online. To examine the approach's performance in posing rotating objects with similar patterns, we create and test it on a newly developed dataset, named Rotating Object Cluster Dataset (ROCD). ROCD consists of 12 different object categories, with 5 objects in each category, and includes 3000 images of rotating objects with various backgrounds. Moreover, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of the approach's scalability with respect to cluster number, and demonstrate that it accurately determines the poses of objects with up to 50 clusters. The implementation and testing of this approach, along with the newly created dataset, also make it suitable for applications involving deep learning, where evaluation protocols and benchmarks play a crucial role, thereby making it an excellent subject for study and exploration. The source code for this paper is available at https://github.com/PranavSingh89/DeepHMap++ and the ROCD dataset is available at https://github.com/PranavSingh89/ROCD. Notably, the star-shaped configuration's stability is influenced by the smallest eigenvalue of a specific trigonal lattice differential operator. Additionally, our analysis includes a formal stability estimate for the star-shaped Euler-Bernoulli beam. This research extends previous findings related to the Euler-Bernoulli plate by showing that a specific, locally extended stability estimate can still serve as an upper bound for the actual stability rate. We validate our analytical findings with numerical simulations. We also explore a corresponding boundary control problem and prove the exact controllability of the star-shaped Euler-Bernoulli beam in a reasonably short time frame. This achievement builds upon previous results for the Euler-Bernoulli plate, demonstrating that a particular, locally extended form of the operator can be precisely controllable through boundary feedback within a comparable time frame. We accompany our analytical proofs with corresponding numerical simulations for both stability and controllability. The purpose of this research is to examine the global stability of the described beam on the specified star-shaped graph. The data also raise important implications for the study of human decision making, highlighting the critical importance of rigorous design and methodological transparency. Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. Although significant progress has been made in NER, there are still considerable challenges remaining, particularly with regards to nested entities. This paper delves into the specifics of nested NER, where entities are nestled within other entities, and proposes a novel graphical model to tackle this complexity. By viewing the entity hierarchy as an entire structural unit, our model incorporates a holistic approach that addresses the challenges associated with nested structures. This approach enables our system to efficiently and effectively identify nested entities by analyzing the entity structure as a whole. This paper provides an in-depth explanation of our approach, as well as a new evaluation metric designed to assess the performance of nested NER systems. This evaluation metric, called F-score, takes into account the accuracy of both the partial matching and the structural consistency of identified entities. Our approach demonstrates state-of-the-art performance across various data sets, consistently outperforming existing state-of-the-art systems by at least 5% in terms of F-score, with improvements reaching as high as 20%. Moreover, our approach exhibits superior performance in handling out-of-vocabulary (OOV) entities, achieving significant gains of at least 10% in OOV detection across all data sets. This improvement in OOV detection is particularly notable because existing systems struggle greatly with detecting such entities. Overall, our approach represents a significant advancement in nested NER, where we describe techniques that enable multiple entities to be matched by a single model, along with a proposed evaluation metric that prioritizes both partial matching and structural accuracy. This approach not only achieves superior performance but also provides a foundation for further research into more complex NER tasks, such as relation extraction and coreference resolution, where entities often form intricate hierarchies. This paper explores possible extensions to such tasks, along with potential future research directions, and makes the source code for our proposed model publicly available on GitHub. This code serves as a starting point for further modifications to handle more complex structures in natural language, where words, phrases, and sentences often form highly nested hierarchies. This paper provides a technical overview of this code, as well as a high-level description of our approach in an explanatory video available on YouTube. This video provides a clear, step-by-step explanation of both our proposed evaluation metric and our model, and is an invaluable resource for anyone looking to understand nested NER and structure-based evaluation methods. This reliance on human data raises concerns about its effectiveness and efficiency. To address these issues, we examine the feasibility of using system-output for training and evaluating these systems. Specifically, we investigate whether using descriptions generated by a single, high-quality source (human or system) can lead to consistent and reliable results across different datasets and populations. Our findings suggest that both human and system-generated descriptions produce inconsistent results, potentially due to variations in description length. Notably, using short descriptions from a single source yields the best results, with an average precision of 20% for recall levels below 0.1. These findings have important implications for the development and assessment of image description systems, highlighting the need for more robust methods that can handle a wide range of descriptions effectively. To this end, we propose a new, description-length-independent measure called subsequence precision, which reflects a system's ability to accurately describe the sequence of objects present in an image. We demonstrate the practical utility of this measure by using it to compare the performance of different systems and describe a new task for the Large-Scale Visual Recognition Challenge (LVIS), whose primary aim is to allow users to generate and share descriptions for a diverse range of categories and objects. Ultimately, we believe that making descriptions more precise and varied will lead to further advancements in image description systems. To achieve this, we suggest a combination of both human and system-generated descriptions, along with the integration of subsequence precision and description length into standard evaluation metrics. Individuals residing in the periphery of major cultural hubs tend to be more susceptible to disseminating misinformation, and this vulnerability is characterized by a lower level of cultural refinement in these areas. This study examines the underlying structure of the information network among Reddit users across the United States and identifies a geographic arrangement of communities that mirrors the principles of Synergetic Cultural Mapping. This phenomenon is attributed to the user's limited cultural capacity to resist the spread of misinformation. Additionally, it was observed that users living in the peripheral regions of these cultural centers are more likely to be exposed to all types of misinformation, while those living in the boundary regions are more likely to be exposed to scientific and health-related misinformation. Furthermore, a analysis of news article networks revealed that users living in the peripheral regions of these cultural centers are more likely to be exposed to misinformation distributed through social networks, while those living in the boundary regions are more likely to be exposed to misinformation distributed via the internet. This study provides a geographic arrangement of subcultures to further understand the spread of misinformation on Reddit and highlights the importance of incorporating cultural factors into the analysis of online information networks. Additionally, it highlights the value of a multidisciplinary approach that combines network analysis, cultural theory, and geography to study the spread of misinformation. Teaching robots via demonstration is an effective and efficient means of providing instructions, but the challenges of interpreting auditory feedback in addition to visual demonstration instructions pose a significant hurdle to learning. In this study, we shift the focus to the auditory component, examining how vocal cues are used by human instructors to communicate while demonstrating various tasks to a robot. Through a qualitative analysis of video recordings featuring humans instructing a robot using both auditory and visual feedback, our data reveals that human instructors use a range of vocal cues, including comments on goal-oriented behavior, descriptions of target objects, and assessments of the robot's performance. Our findings also indicate that humans employ different acoustic patterns to describe different aspects of the demonstration, with a particular emphasis on expressing satisfaction or dissatisfaction with the robot's actions, its grasp on objects, the success or failure of the demonstration, and any necessary corrections. In addition, we have developed a comprehensive framework that categorizes acoustic patterns of human instruction as either goal-oriented or auxiliary, with further sub-classifications for specific contexts. This theoretical framework provides a sound foundation for future research aimed at developing automated detection methods for acoustic patterns, which in turn can enhance the evaluation and learning capabilities of robots taught through demonstration. In this study, we introduce an initial metric for evaluating the comprehension of robot-learning algorithms in relation to acoustic patterns, and we showcase the effectiveness of this metric using a simple machine-learning approach. In conclusion, we highlight the significance of sound in human-robot demonstration learning and propose potential applications, such as the development of more effective robot instructors, as well as sound-based feedback mechanisms. In addition, we provide a repository containing our dataset and a demonstration protocol that can be used by other researchers working in this domain. Furthermore, we introduce a new challenge related to the detection of action-related acoustic feedback, which provides a clear problem statement, a set of rules governing protocol adherence, and a description of suitable evaluation metrics. This challenge can be used as a benchmark to assess the performance of robot-learning algorithms. Through this study, we aim to contribute to the expansion of rich and nuanced demonstration protocols that incorporate both visual and auditory feedback, which in turn can lead to the development of more effective and robust robot-learning algorithms. In conclusion, we believe that the sound produced by human instructors holds significant value and deserves close attention from researchers working in the human-robot learning community. As a result, we propose the term "acoustic protocol" to describe the sound produced by humans during demonstration instructions, with a corresponding set of protocol rules that outline the appropriate use of sound in this context

This study examines the mathematical complexity of geometric field theories, focusing on theories that satisfy a specific integro-differential criterion. Theoretical models that fail to meet this standard are analyzed in order to understand the underlying reasons for their geometric complexity. The discussion centers on the Chern-Weil approach and its connection to the Euler-Arnold equations. The geometric complexity of a field theory is shown to arise from the interplay between the theory's integral form and the geometry of the underlying manifold. The discussion also highlights the role of symmetry in simplifying the geometry of complex field theories. The relationship between geometric complexity and the associated Hamiltonian vector field is also examined. The primary challenge in applying neural machine translation (NMT) to low-resource languages includes the limited availability of parallel corpora. A significant issue here is that existing NMT methods struggle to leverage monolingual data effectively. Despite its considerable size, parallel corpora are often insufficient to train a robust translation model for a specific language pair. To overcome this, we propose a novel framework called Neural Machine Rendering, which incorporates a monolingual translation archive to guide the rendering process. By using this approach, we successfully trained high-quality English-$arabic$ translation models using approximately 2 million English-French parallel corpora and a vast archive of English-monolingual data, thereby extending the application of NMT to low-resource language pairs like Arabic. Our experiments demonstrate substantial improvements in translation accuracy for several low-resource language pairs, including Arabic, Punjabi, and Japanese, with significant gains in BLEU scores reaching +1.16 BLEU compared to standard NMT models. Our archive-based model also achieved marked success in generating diverse translations and outperformed state-of-the-art methods like zero-shot translation and machine-in-the-loop by a substantial margin of 5.3 in BLEU. Furthermore, our results show that our archive-based model performs well on difficult sentences that standard NMT methods struggle with, thereby indicating its potential as a versatile NMT model suitable for various applications and tasks. Our archive-based model's ability to process approximately 2-10 sentences per second on a single GPU makes it suitable for practical use. Additionally, our findings indicate that our archive-based model's effectiveness is largely independent of the size of the monolingual data used, thereby providing it as a suitable basis for further research on the incorporation of large-scale monolingual data in NMT systems. Finally, our results provide valuable insights on the use of monolingual data in NMT that could serve as a foundation for exploring ways to integrate auxiliary tasks that promote diversity and quality in NMT systems. Additionally, we introduce a novel evaluation metric called tokenized BLEU with no lower-bound issue, which is more accurate than standard BLEU in evaluating the quality of translations. Our archive-based model's code and data are available online at https://github.com/ghr52/NMR. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multiple sparse domains without any well-supplied domains. In line with human behavior, we propose a Multi-Appearance Thresholding algorithm to capture a natural distribution where users' preferences follow a two-mode pattern: a narrow favorite area and a broader acceptable range. We introduce a Thresholding Cross-Domain Preference Network (TCDPN) that leverages a unique feature binding method and a contrastive learning technique to enhance the robustness of preference models across domains. Furthermore, we developed a Domain Adaptation module with low additional computational overhead to facilitate cross-domain learning. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate the MSDCR's superiority over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. The analysis of user preference datasets provides insights that can inform system designers and practitioners, and the study's results are relevant to various recommender system applications, such as personalized product recommendations, movie and TV show suggestions, and tailored news feeds. The implemented MSDCR framework achieves high performance on actual deployment metrics, such as click-through rates and sales conversion, outperforming existing methods by up to 15%. The enhanced details achieved by MRI protocols are crucial for diagnosing medical conditions accurately. However, the long scanning time affects patient comfort and limits the wide-spread use of MRI in clinical settings. To optimize imaging quality within restricted time frames, we investigate the potential for automated data-driven methods to adapt MRI protocols, overcoming significant challenges such as minimizing dimensions, reducing scattering, and selecting the most effective encoding strategies. By experimenting with a range of protocols, including parallel acquisition, reduced echo spacing, and contrast enhancement, we find that small changes in protocol dimensions do not significantly impact image quality, while a more substantial increase in scatter leads to poor image clarity. Interestingly, encoded information can preserve or distort tissue contrast, resulting in sub-optimal image quality when specific encoding strategies are used. To demonstrate the feasibility of optimizing MRI protocols, we model the problem using a multi-dimensional optimization framework and successfully test it on reconstructed MRI images. The optimized protocols achieved a notable 50% reduction in scanning time while minimizing the loss in image quality, underscoring the potential of data-driven methods to enhance MRI efficacy. The case for further research in this area is strong, given the abundant MRI datasets available and the promising results obtained. The potential breakthroughs in clinical and biomedical research that could be achieved by optimizing MRI protocols in various applications also present an exciting research direction. Unlike the usual categorical semantics method, our approach incorporates the principles of categorical geometry to analyze the connectives' effects on sentences' truth values. In a category of vector spaces, we show how to interpret the usual unary connectives (negation, disjunction, conjunction, implication) in a meaningful way, but with a crucial difference: their interactions no longer follow the expected laws of classical logic. Instead, our interpreted language exhibits a form of "twisted" logic, characterized by the satisfaction of intuitive coherence conditions that reflect the geometric relationships between truth values. This twist raises intriguing questions about the relationship between language and world, inviting further exploration of our proposed framework's consequences and potential extensions. Specifically, we explore how our interpreted language captures the intuitive idea that the truth of certain statements depends on the relative positions of certain vectors, leading to the emergence of a higher-dimensional analog of the law of excluded middle. Moreover, we demonstrate how our category of twisted vector spaces can be seen as a category of families of traditional vector spaces, utilizing this connection to provide a more concise algebraic representation of our interpreted language's connectives. This representation, in turn, enables us to reconstruct the original truth values of sentences using their connectives, but with an interesting twist: the resulting statements can be seen as describing the geometric properties of specific hyperplanes in a linear space, rather than the space as a whole. This insight gives rise to a deeper appreciation of the relationships between the connectives' intuitive meanings, their geometric interpretations, and the abstract semantic structure of our interpreted language. To facilitate a broader exploration of our proposed framework, we also outline a strategy for developing a higher-order version of our interpreted language, along with a new interpretation of our connectives as operations on sets of truth values, inspired by the principles of a well-known theory in mathematics. This approach, in turn, raises interesting questions about the relationship between our interpreted language and this higher-order language, involving both its connectives and its semantics. Ultimately, our research lays the groundwork for an innovative blend of categorical semantics, linear geometry, and logical interpretation, offering a valuable resource for those seeking to explore the connections between these fields or to develop new interpretations of linguistic operations. We face a significant challenge in designing algorithms for multiagent learning in noncooperative settings, as the vast array of possible equilibria in multiplayer games complicates our task. In this study, we introduce a new, broader class of rationalizable equilibria that is learnable in a multiagent context through a simple and efficient procedure. This class, called "approximately independent optimal" (AIO) equilibria, reflects real-world observations, such as the prevalence of AIO equilibria in online auctions and markets. We demonstrate that AIO equilibria can be learned using a novel approach called the "independent sample" mechanism, which allows each agent to induce a standalone problem that mirrors the original game at a comparable rate. Although this approach may seem divergent, we prove that it yields a mechanism that convergently learns AIO policies and, in turn, AIO equilibria. We validate our approach through extensive experiments in both simulated and real-world data, showing that it effectively learns optimal AIO prices in online auctions. Notably, our approach achieves superior performance to multiple state-of-the-art methods in these experiments. We also observe that many real-world datasets containing rich contextual features, such as online auction data and market transactions, often contain a high percentage of AIO actions. In fact, we discover that as much as 93% of Amazon Mechanical Turk payments correspond to AIO labels in a particular classification task. Our results suggest that our approach's effectiveness may rely on its ability to learn from datasets featuring a high proportion of AIO actions. We anticipate that our findings will contribute to the further exploration of multiagent learning in the context of noncooperative games and may inspire the design of new algorithms capable of learning from a wide range of rationalizable equilibria. We believe that our approach can be applied to learn optimal policies in multiplayer context games, such as the study of human behavior in social dilemmas and online cooperation. This transition is associated with an increasing spin diffusion length in the LaNiO$_3$ layer below 150 K. This analysis was conducted as a training exercise for participants in the 2019 International Open Week, who were challenged to explore 18 different traits using the functional genomics platform FunDOr.  Our results reveal that certain genomic regions with established associations with a particular trait also show evidence of being functionally active, as indicated by their enrichment in specific genomic features considered important for that trait.  Conversely, we found that certain genomic features linked to a trait did not appear related to it based on functional genomics data, or vice versa.  Our analysis also uncovered correlations between traits that share common genomic features or functional activities.  We would like to express our gratitude to the open access initiatives that made available the vast amount of biomedical data used in this analysis, and we hope that our results will inspire further exploration of the traits examined here using the FunDOr platform.  We are also pleased to announce that the FunDOr platform will be used as a tool for instruction and research during the upcoming International Open Week, and we invite anyone to join us in exploring the human genome through open access to biomedical data. Observations of gamma-ray bursters and X-ray binaries have revealed a significant population of compact binaries that form when a neutron star or black hole sustains matter from a companion star. Some of these systems go through transient outbursts characterized by rapid X-ray fluctuations. Research has identified two primary types of transients: SNe-like events and non-SNe like events, distinguished by their absolute magnitudes and likelihood of future explosions. A distinct subgroup within the non-SNe like category exhibits prolonged intervals between separate outbursts, referred to as the repetition interval. A new study by Serafimovich and Tsvetkov offers an alternative explanation for these long intervals, suggesting they result from the companion star expelling matter in a stellar outburst, followed by a phase where the binary system appears as an inactive low-mass X-ray binary until another transient event occurs. This hypothesis is supported by data showing a strong correlation between the binary system's period and the duration of their outbursts, as well as evidence of matter being drained from the companion star during each transient event. Additionally, this research implies that a significant proportion of dormant compact binaries in the Milky Way should exhibit outbursts at any moment, using the known population of neutron star binaries and X-ray transients as a basis. Using this approach, it is estimated that approximately 20-30% of 30 known dormant Galactic Center neutron star binaries and X-ray binaries will experience an outburst within the next decade. Furthermore, it is predicted that about half of these outbursts will occur over the next century, providing several targets for future outburst predictions and multi-wavelength observations of these events. Finally, it is suggested that wide neutron star binaries, located in the Greater Magellanic Cloud, may explain a notable repetition pattern observed in the X-ray binary system XTE J1113-609. Overall, this research uncovers a new understanding of the dynamics underlying neutron star binary transients and reveals a prominent population of matter-acceting neutron stars that form from companion stars with a mass greater than 0.5 times the mass of the Sun. This discovery also implies a more extensive presence of neutron star binaries in the Milky Way, with approximately 100-400 such systems containing a mature companion that are too distant or too aligned to emit detectable pulsar signals. Finally, this study offers a new explanation for the absence of any recorded short-duration gamma-ray bursts from the Galactic Center, suggesting that an extremely close and compact binary system would produce a short-duration explosion.

Kernel-based methods have proven highly effective in various tasks like classification, reinforcement learning, and feature extraction, particularly when combined with neural networks. However, a significant hurdle in their application is the need to fix the kernel function before training, which can lead to an inefficient use of data. This issue is addressed by introducing a novel data-dependent kernel estimator known as the Random Fourier Attribute (RFA) kernel. This estimator takes advantage of the fact that neural network-based features can be seen as a collection of sinusoidal functions with optimal frequencies. By utilizing these frequencies to compute the pairwise correlations between data points, the RFA kernel achieves state-of-the-art performance in comparison to fixed kernel methods and reduces the necessity for hyperparameter tuning. Additionally, the RFA kernel serves as a transparent explanation for the neural network's decision-making process. Furthermore, we introduce an optimized version of the RFA kernel called the Optimized Random Fourier Attribute (ORFA) kernel, which utilizes the neural network's output to compute a data-dependent set of frequencies. This optimized kernel results in a significant improvement in performance for complex classification tasks. Both the RFAs and ORFAs demonstrate robustness to overfitting and are compatible with regularization techniques. Moreover, we introduce an alternative formulation for the ORFA kernel that is computationally efficient, making it suitable for applications involving extensive computational costs. This new formulation is known as the Optimized Random Fourier Attribute with Bias (ORFAB) kernel. This ORFAB kernel is not only computationally efficient but also offers a level of flexibility in hyperparameter selection. This is further evidenced by the fact that the ORFAB kernel's data-dependent nature allows it to select the optimal set of frequencies that minimize a predefined loss function. This property is particularly useful in problems involving multiple classes, where the ORFAB kernel is capable of identifying the most distinct features across all classes. This is achieved by assigning a higher importance weight to the attributes with the most significant inter-class variations. This weighted strategy for the ORFAB kernel is found to significantly outperform the existing state-of-the-art methods in our experiments. Building upon this, we propose a neural model that learns from the strengths of both approaches. By leveraging the extensive training of $n$-gram models and incorporating their knowledge into a neural network through residual learning, we achieve significant improvements in both test sets and computational resources. Our process involves training $n$-gram models on vast training datasets, reducing their complexity through feature selection, and then integrating this compact, high-quality knowledge into a neural network. Utilizing this approach, we experience improved computational efficiency along with enhanced performance on various metrics. We apply this method to sentence creation, a critical aspect of neural text generation, and our results show notable gains in both automatic and human evaluations. Notably, our approach outperforms neural models in efficiency and matches or surpasses their performance. We also explore the effects of our method on word choice, finding that it leads to more diverse selections. Overall, our approach combines the best aspects of both $n$-gram models and neural networks, resulting in a more effective and efficient sentence creation system. We believe this method can also be adapted for other text generation tasks like summarization and conversation. Our code is available at https://github.com/hkz2018/res-ngram. To regulate this choice, we suggest developing a more dynamic framework that adapts to changes in $n$-gram models by incorporating their internal state. This kind of optimized code is expected to produce even better outcomes. In order to facilitate further research, I plan to expand on this project by exploring the following areas. Firstly, I will broaden the scope to be more comprehensive in regards to neural network architectures. Secondly, I will conduct more extensive research on multiple text creation tasks. Lastly, I will investigate ways to integrate our approach with other models like transformer-xlarge and model ensembles. Although the effect of our method on word choice variety has shown promising results, it still requires more substantial validation. To achieve this, I will carry out more sophisticated analyses on both automatic and human evaluations. Moreover, I will explore the impact of our approach on other important aspects of sentence creation such as grammaticality and coherence.

The proposed framework demonstrates its benefits in real-world scenarios, showcasing an average efficiency gain of 10% in energy planning compared to traditional approaches. Experimental results show this framework's effectiveness in enhancing the word embedding of PWS and its applicability to various WSD tasks.  The proposed framework is named Context-gloss Enhanced Module (CEM), and it outperforms several state-of-the-art baselines in various WSD tasks. In contrast to traditional few-shot learning, OPL shifts the perspective from isolating groups to integrating emerging categories within existing ones. As a result, our benchmark incorporates a comprehensive framework that combines classification and generation components to represent the ongoing learning process. The former involves modeling existing categories with high accuracy, while the latter involves adapting to novel categories with minimal data. To facilitate this benchmark, we developed a unique dataset that combines text-to-class and text-to-generate tasks, utilizing a large linguistic dataset with intrinsic relationships between categories. Our results demonstrate the challenges posed by OPL, revealing limitations in both continuous few-shot learning and ongoing classification. Furthermore, we showcase the potential of this benchmark to guide the development of more effective continuous learning methods. In line with open research practices, all code and models used in this study are publicly accessible, and we invite the community to collaborate and contribute to this challenge. This study presents radio recombination lines (RRL) observed by the Green Bank Telescope for 17 Seyfert galaxies. We analyzed these lines to determine line widths and shapes, and compared them to wide, narrow, and double-component models. Our results show that wide models fit most of the lines well, indicating that RRL widths are primarily affected by gas velocity dispersion rather than line width. We found a correlation between wide models' line widths and host galaxy velocity dispersions. Furthermore, we detected unusual, double-component lines in 5 Seyfert galaxies and proposed a model where these lines result from shock-induced ionization. Our analysis suggests that these shock-ionized regions are often oriented perpendicular to the primary ionization axis caused by the active galactic nucleus. This may indicate that multiple ionization patterns can coexist in these galaxies. Additionally, we observed a larger scale of double-component line widths and shapes, suggesting a global veiling of gas ionized by the active nucleus. This is in agreement with previous findings regarding [O III] veiling. We also discovered a larger spread in narrow model line widths when considering the veiling effect, which could be linked to gas dynamics influenced by a massive central black hole. Overall, this study provides further evidence that a wider angle of ionization exists beyond the primary axis and a larger scale of veiling in these galaxies. This veiling may be linked to the relationship between the active nucleus and its surroundings and could result from a powerful outflow or a larger scale interaction with the host galaxy's potential. This study expands our knowledge of a larger scale of veiling in Seyfert galaxies and it is possible that a similar veiling exists in Low Ionization Narrow Emission Line (LINER) galaxies, which are typically closer to us. Therefore, observing RRL in these galaxies could provide valuable information about their ionization and velocity fields. Lastly, we detected a large velocity gradient in the Seyfert galaxy Mrk 79 and proposed an explanation involving a global veiling and shock-ionization, which is consistent with previous findings regarding this galaxy's [O III] emission. This galaxy exhibits the largest velocity gradient among all the Seyfert galaxies studied and it is worth further examination using radio continuum and optical observations. On a Cayley tree, we define a special type of Ising model that has novel weakly periodic Gibbs distributions. These distributions represent the equilibrium state of the system when it is connected to two identical heat sources located at the two ends of the tree. We show that, unlike traditional periodic Gibbs distributions which are extremely sensitive to small changes in temperature, the novel weakly periodic distributions can be robust against minor temperature differences. Additionally, in the novel distributions, the order parameter at any given node is not independent, being determined by a simpler condition related to the node's degree. This intricate dependence of the system's behavior on the connectivity of the tree raises interesting questions about the breakdown of periodic states when the tree becomes random. Finally, we observe that the novel periodic distributions correspond to a system where the interaction strength between any two nodes gradually decreases as the distance between them increases. This unnatural behavior, however, does not impede the existence of novel periodic states. We also propose a related problem involving the placement of spins on a d-dimensional grid, and offer a solution for the case of a thin grid. This solution reveals a novel periodic state, which we call a "rosette state," and demonstrates that it can be robust. Furthermore, we establish a link between these states and a system of coupled oscillators. This connection, however, is lost when the grid becomes a regular lattice in three or more dimensions. In such cases, the novel periodic states can only exist at very low temperatures, and at these temperatures, the system behaves in an irregular manner, contrary to our expectations. This unexpected outcome raises the question of whether there is a more refined version of this phenomenon, and if it might occur again at very high temperatures. This study provides a mathematical framework for analyzing the Ising model on any type of graph, and pinpoints the conditions required for a novel periodic state to emerge. This knowledge, however, does not address the more complex issue of whether these states can also occur in actual magnetic materials. It is essential to distinguish between the theoretical state represented by this model, and the observed phenomena in materials that are often described by this model. In such cases, the novel periodic states often cannot be accounted for by a simple adjustment of the model's parameters, and may instead indicate a need for a more fundamental change in our understanding of the material's behavior. This study offers a new perspective on the Ising model, and we hope that it will provide a useful framework for exploring even more complex models. A collective ergodic theory is established for a family of ergodic systems identified by online identity numbers, enabling the generation of approximately true predictions for an vast number of ergodic systems. A crucial aspect is the development of a novel filtering method, using matrix Pad\'e approximations and random matrix theory, to accurately determine the distinct identity numbers of independent systems. This method significantly improves previous filters, such as the R\'enyi inequality-based filter, by producing more reliable results in line with theoretical expectations. In particular, we show that the new filter's errors decrease in proportion to $n^{-1}$ for $n$-dimensional systems, in contrast to $n^{-1/4}$ for the R\'enyi inequality-based filter. As a consequence, the collective ergodic theory can learn from a significantly smaller number of systems. In addition, we introduce a new algorithm that leverages this improved filter to accurately determine the correct number of independent systems from a large set of observed time series data. This algorithm's performance is demonstrated through numerical experiments using synthetic and real-world data, showcasing its capability to accurately determine the number of independent systems even when there are many ergodic systems. Furthermore, we apply this algorithm to successfully predict stock market prices and volume, achieving significant improvements over previous models. The source code for the algorithm is available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/series-learning/collective-ergodicity. The novel filter and collective ergodic theory algorithm provide a framework for enhancing the performance of models relying on independent components, and is potentially applicable to a broad range of domains involving time series data. In addition, we highlight the potential of this framework to enhance the performance of other machine learning methods, through an example prediction of a time series generated by multiple ergodic systems, using a neural network. The results demonstrate the ability of the collective ergodic theory algorithm to produce a model performing better than a model learned from a large number of independent systems, despite the fact that the true identity numbers of the generating systems are known. This suggests that this framework could be generally useful for improving the performance when dealing with time series data generated by multiple independent components. Based on comprehensive experiments, our analysis reveals that 3D bounding boxes in far distances have significantly broader variations in orientation, larger depth, and narrower height compared to closer objects. Taking these observations into account, we introduce Far3Det, a 3D detection framework specifically designed for distant objects. In developing Far3Det, we take a multi-stage approach, initially using angular-robust 3D boxes to capture the wide range of orientations in far objects. As objects in far distances have inherent depth information, we incorporate this information into the detection process through a dedicated front-end LiDAR scanner. Furthermore, we introduce a novel score function tailored to evaluate the accuracy of distant objects, along with a new evaluation metric called IOU3D@K which effectively assesses the performance of detectors at far distances. Our findings show that Far3Det achieves superior results on the LU-360 dataset, outperforming existing 3D detectors by a significant margin on distant objects, while also demonstrating the practical applications of the method through real-world scenarios. During operation, a Timeloops agent within the application's container continuously monitors system calls made to the host machine and creates a simple rule set for future instances of the application. We have successfully tested this approach with various container networks and demonstrated that Timeloops' rule-based calls prevent unauthorized interactions with the host, achieving similar results to Linux's Seccomp filter with significantly less administrative effort. Furthermore, we have found that rule creation is already efficient enough for typical web and media applications, and we have established a framework for optimizing rule generation for other applications. The development and evaluation of this method have shown that it is an effective and user-friendly solution for secure system call rule management. The source code of our project is now available on GitHub under the Apache-2.0 license. We have already incorporated improvements suggested by several reviewers and users into the latest version of the code. To facilitate further research, we have also established a new benchmark suite consisting of ten diverse applications and have made it freely downloadable from our project website. The name "Timeloops" is derived from the combination of the terms "time" and "loops," referring to the monitoring of system calls made over a specific time period and the repetitive nature of loops in program code. The primary goal of this research is to provide a suitable solution for the system call rule management challenge facing cloud and edge computing environments. The issue with existing system call rule methods is their reliance on precise static analysis of application code, which is often impractical due to the complexity of modern software architectures. In contrast, the Timeloops approach creates secure system call rules dynamically while the application is running, eliminating the need for time-consuming static analysis. This method involves training a machine learning model to predict the safety of system calls made by an application based on specific time periods, or "timeloops." The development of this method involved establishing a dataset of safe and unsafe system calls for reference applications, training the machine learning model using this data, and conducting a threat analysis to mitigate potential system call-related security vulnerabilities. The effectiveness of this method was verified through a security audit of 16 applications trained with the Timeloops Model, the Timeloops developer guide, and the evaluation of this method is also discussed. In high-stakes situations of soccer games, the team that adapts best to changing circumstances tends to have the greatest luck. This insight guides our approach to developing automated soccer strategies that are resilient and adaptable for the critical phases of a match. By incorporating a dynamic analysis of the game's progression and using a reinforcement learning algorithm to optimize strategic decisions, we were able to demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in comparing teams through a fair competitive framework. The results of our experiments show that our automated strategies outperform randomly generated ones and hold a significant advantage over established methods from the field of artificial intelligence. Furthermore, we discovered that the strength of our approach lies in its ability to make prudent substitutions, utilize set pieces efficiently, and defend against opponents' attacks. We were also able to apply our method to analyze the strategies employed by real soccer teams during the 2018-2019 European Championship, drawing intriguing insights from that analysis. By examining the statistics of soccer teams' strategies, we were able to use our model to make predictions about the outcome of games, showing a level of accuracy comparable to other predictive models. Our approach has the potential to be expanded to other sports by adapting the game dynamics and implementing a proper competitive framework. With this in mind, we have made our code available on GitHub, utilizing Python with the PyTorch and Scipy libraries. This implementation is based on the RLFS framework, a simple and flexible library for creating reinforcement learning algorithms in Python. We have also included a detailed guide on how to use the code and a set of pre-trained models for easy reference. To study the interplay between geographical displacement and competition for survival, we introduced a voter model with a competition-colonization balance in a two-dimensional non-repeating landscape. Our analysis reveals that when the model reaches a stationary state, it exhibits a coexistence pattern, whereas temporary dominance patterns emerge in the model's transient phase. Our findings show that in the stationary state, species with an advantage over others are not guaranteed to dominate and eliminate the competition, whereas in the transient phase, species with a colonial advantage will almost surely dominate and the probability of surviving without a colonial advantage decreases with time. Additionally, increasing colonization rates leads to increased probability of species survival without a colonial advantage in the transient phase, while decreasing competition rates has the opposite effect. Our research also demonstrates that in the stationary state, species with a colonial advantage will not dominate over competitors at sufficiently low colonization rates, and that there are specific competition and colonization rate conditions for coexistence, species elimination, or the transient phase in the model's dynamics. This research focuses on an integrated radio frequency (RF) networkcomprising two types of nodes: Intellect Reflecting Surface (IRS) units and conventional access points. The IRS units have the ability to dynamically adjust their surface properties to optimize signal reflection, giving them adaptive reflecting power. This capability allows for the seamless integration of wireless communication and power transfer, while facilitating spatial reuse and increasing network coverage. Our study analyzes three scenarios based on the location of source signals and wireless communication/ power transfer transmitters. For the selected scenario, we develop an optimization framework that utilizes convex optimization to determine the optimal surface design, transmit powers, and node locations, subject to the constraints of signal reception quality, wireless communication, and power transfer efficiency. Moreover, we propose a novel application called Intellect Reflecting Surface-Assisted Integrated Data and Power Networking (IRSI DN), characterized by a multi-RIS setup, variable access point locations, and a binary on/off switch for wireless communication and power transfer transmitters. This IRS DN system offers enhanced coverage, expanded network coverage area, and increased network coverage through optimized surface design, transmit power, and node locations. Finally, we numerically evaluate the proposed IRS DN system and observe significant improvements in network performance, coverage extension, and optimized design, showcasing the effectiveness of our approach. This research provides a theoretical foundation for the development of integrated RF networks, and we outline potential avenues for further research on the IRS DN technology. In addition, we explore the potential of extending this technology to other applications and we outline the technical challenges that need to be addressed in the development of advanced communication systems. Finally, we provide an overview of relevant research areas that could benefit from the proposed methodology. While LDV (Laser-Doppler velocity measurement) technology is highly accurate for measuring flow velocities, its limited sampling area can pose challenges. To overcome this limitation, researchers have implemented various methods to scan the measurement area, including mechanized beams and scanning systems. However, these approaches often compromise on precision by introducing errors, particularly when measuring in two-dimensional spaces. This paper introduces a solution involving the remote control of a single-point LDV system via a computer-controlled swivel table and additional mechanical components. By precisely controlling the movement of these elements, a predetermined pattern can be achieved across the measured area, thereby minimizing potential errors and allowing for precise two-dimensional velocity measurements. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this solution, the paper includes results from measuring the velocity of a turbulent flow in a two-dimensional space. Additionally, it explores the possibility of applying this method to measure velocities in three-dimensional spaces. Furthermore, the paper examines the capability of this setup to detect changes in flow patterns by incorporating an optoelectronic 2D anemometer that can measure static flow patterns. The introduction of this device also enables the detection of areas with zero-velocity measurements, which can be incorporated into the measurement algorithm. The paper concludes by analyzing the feasibility of utilizing this setup for mapping global velocities in three-dimensional spaces. The provided data and software for the presented methodology can be found at the mentioned repository. Overall, this paper offers a solution for accurately obtaining two-dimensional velocity measurements with a single-point LDV system through the remote control of the system's scanning components. The introduced approach may also be adapted for the distant control of other precision measurement devices, enabling them to make precise two-dimensional measurements. The paper provides a technical overview suitable for a broad audience, in addition to a deeper theoretical analysis appropriate for a specialized audience. This article takes a detailed mathematical approach to explain the functioning of this disk and demonstrates its equivalence to two independent quadrature surfaces. We also provide theoretical optimization techniques to enhance its performance by adjusting the disk's shape to counteract aberrations, specifically anisotropic ones. Furthermore, this article provides a practical implementation guide for users to manually correct their TEM using a programmable phase disk through a related journal article. We have previously shown the effectiveness of this method in reducing stray light to less than one part in ten thousand. The cross-modal attention mechanism in generative conversation models allows users to control the generation of the response partner by specifying the speaker. However, the information about the speaker is only incorporated into the encoder that prepares the speaker's message for input, not the decoder that generates the response. The question arises of whether the encoder's representation of the speaker's message contains all the information necessary to deduce the speaker's identity. To investigate this, we conduct a series of experiments to examine the ability of both the encoder and the decoder to predict the speaker's assignment. The results show that the encoder's performance in this task is actually inferior to the decoder's, indicating that the encoder's representation of the speaker's message does not convey sufficient information to deduce the speaker's identity. Furthermore, the disparity in the scores further suggests that the better performance of the decoder is not simply a reflection of its greater complexity. The findings of our analysis that the differences in the scores are not reflected in the speaker classification accuracy, however, raise questions about the practical implications of this discrepancy. In total, our experiments provide strong evidence that the information about the speaker's assignment is not adequately captured by the encoder's representation of the speaker's message. Deep Learning (DL) techniques have seen a significant surge in application across automation sectors including autonomous vehicles, where they are utilized for recognizing locations using 3D LiDAR data. However, a significant hurdle in this process is the time-consuming and exhaustive dataset creation process necessary for training these models. This issue becomes even more pronounced when we consider the diverse range of locations that need to be identified, making it challenging to cover all scenarios thoroughly. In this research, we leverage cutting-edge DL techniques, specifically self-supervised learning and segmentation, to develop a novel framework, named AttDLNet, which is capable of learning from partial 3D LiDAR points cloud data. This framework is particularly designed to identify 12 fundamental locations within a room, such as corners and mid-points between walls and the entrance/exit, from raw 3D LiDAR data without the need for annotated training datasets. Our results demonstrate that AttDLNet achieves accurate location recognition on both real and virtual datasets, outperforming existing state-of-the-art approaches, and significantly reducing the necessary 3D LiDAR data required for training. Moreover, a module for evaluating the framework's performance and a comprehensive experimental analysis are also detailed. Furthermore, we find that AttDLNet's performance is robust in the presence of various environmental disturbances and is capable of adapting to different room layouts. Additionally, we explore the integration of additional data, such as 2D lidar data or GPS coordinates, on top of the core 3D LiDAR location recognition module. This research contributes a reputable repository of open-source code and a comprehensive dataset based on real-world 3D LiDAR data, both of which are made publicly available for further development and extension of location recognition systems. This was done by developing a semi-classical model for the heat transfer process and deriving a long-wavelength approximation. This approximation leads to a specific energy expression that represents the heat transfer process, which is equivalent to the response of a specific energy system to an external electric potential. This equivalence enables us to extract the heat transfer properties from the energy expression. In particular cases, such as the doping of a specific type (Kronenberger doping), the heat transfer response is directly related to the doping's effect on the energy system. Additionally, we found that the heat transfer speed in doped graphene can be both increased and decreased, depending on the temperature and type of doping. For example, a high temperature and a specific type of doping (such as the Kronenberger doping) can significantly slow down the heat transfer, while a low temperature and another type of doping (such as the resonance doping) can speed it up. The methods we used to analyze the heat transfer process may also be applicable to other systems composed of closely-packed rings. The results of our study can be experimentally verified using a combination of existing techniques. The findings of this research may lead to the development of new heat management technologies. The description of heat transfer in doped graphene challenges the common assumption that the heat transfer process is a local phenomenon. The heat transfer process is not local in doped graphene because the energy systems that make it up are highly interconnected, which gives this material some unique properties. The heat transfer process in doped graphene is more complex than in other materials because it involves a mix of both local and non-local processes. The common approach to studying heat transfer is based on the heat diffusion equation, which describes the local process of heat spreading out from a hot spot. Recent advances in machine translation have motivated the development of sequential generation models for tasks such as speech generation, which pose particular challenges due to their linear structure and the need for contextual context. To address this, our proposed MaskedSpeech model builds on existing sequential generation models by incorporating a vertical masking mechanism. This allows the model to effectively capture contextual information by generating each sentence element from a broader context, rather than the previous element alone. Through extensive experiments on the LJSpeech dataset, our MaskedSpeech model has shown superior performance to baseline models and a notable 20% reduction in word error rate when evaluated on the GLUE dataset. Furthermore, our analysis of the masking mechanism's impact has revealed that it promotes the use of contextual syntax and parts of speech. Additionally, we found that introducing a horizontal unmasking mechanism, which enables the model to generate the next element from the previous one, can be an effective way to address difficulties with sentence start words. Our work has implications for the development of context-aware sequential generation models and has been integrated into the popular transformer-based BART model. The source code for our MaskedSpeech model has been made publicly available on GitHub. Moreover, our experiments have been replicated and new additional results have been obtained, making the repository an up-to-date version of our study. Specifically, we have achieved a word error rate of 0.44 on the GLUE dataset and a frequency error rate of 0.28 on the LJSpeech dataset. The models used in these experiments have been integrated into the mask-speech toolkit, along with their respective parameters and hyperparameters. This toolkit provides flexible multi-node training and evaluation capabilities for the MaskedSpeech model. Furthermore, we have obtained a significant 0.06 reduction in word error rate achieved with a horizontal unmasking approach and a 0.3 reduction in frequency error rate with a vertical unmasking approach. The improved models used in these experiments have been made available on the GitHub repository along with the mask-speech toolkit. We derive new conclusions regarding the additive Galois module properties of specific wildly ramified finite extensions of Q. Notably, in cases where K is a non-commutative Galois extension of Q with a specific type of ramification, we determine the structure of its additive Galois group. Additionally, we establish the isomorphism between the additive Galois group of a certain cyclic extension of Q and a specific group related to a Z16 subring, which is an application of our initial findings. These conclusions build upon earlier work by Leopoldt, who primarily focused on commutative extensions. Our results also provide a new explanation for the complexity bounds observed in computer-based calculations of the integers behind a particular real algebraic number when K is associated with this number's minimal polynomial. 
Finally, we conclude this project by examining potential generalizations of our findings to a broader class of finite extensions of Q. While certain bases for elements of a finite extension of Q are introduced, which are analogous to those defined by Leopoldt, they may not be compatible with the definition of a Galois module structure. Therefore, we are led to a more general definition of a Galois module, which is then shown to be applicable when the base field is a number field, but it holds for an infinite number of primes when the base field is Q. In contrast, when the base field is Q, the defined Galois module structure does not depend on the choice of the base field. Furthermore, all previously mentioned conclusions regarding the structure of the additive Galois group remain valid for an infinite number of primes.

In experiments involving particle collisions, identifying neutral particles like axion-like particles (ALPs) is challenging because they seldom interact with detectors. Under certain conditions of electrodynamics, ALPs can be detected indirectly by observing the decay of other particles into light, which then converts into ALPs that might not be detected directly. Within the framework of the Belle II experiment at an electron positron collider, our research focuses on the decay of certain bottom mesons, specifically $\Upsilon(1S)$ decays into two electrons, or $\bar{p}p$ final states, where the expected number of ALP events ranges from 0 to approximately 0.5 event per $10^9$ $\Upsilon(1S)$ decays. Given various production and detection processes, we develop a statistical method to evaluate the Belle II experiment's sensitivity to ALPs, taking into account any limitations imposed by the experiment's ability to identify certain particles. Furthermore, we investigate different possible signatures of ALP production, particularly in rare $B$ decays, and show that the Belle II experiment will have significant sensitivity to a broad range of ALP masses. For instance, in the case of the rare decay $B^+\to \bar{p}-l^+-\nu$, depending on the lepton type, the experiment will be able to detect ALPs with masses ranging from $0.0013$ GeV to $0.0044$ GeV, or with a mass of $0.014$ GeV in the case of the decay $\Upsilon(1S)\to \bar{p}\gamma$. These results highlight the Belle II experiment's significant discovery potential in searching for ALPs through a variety of production and detection processes. These frameworks have enhanced the capacity of machine learning models to identify and grasp language context, thereby improving the performance of various NLP tasks. Despite their overall benefits, there has been limited research into contextualized language frameworks and their application to semantic spam detection. To address this research gap, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of contextualized language frameworks in relation to this particular issue. Specifically, we examined contextualized language frameworks from three perspectives: the underlying architecture of the frameworks, the pre-trained task of search engine rank normalization, and the characteristic of spam detectors that are trained on data with inferred semantic alterations. Our research revealed that certain contextualized language frameworks with robust core architectures, capable of capturing long-distance dependencies and complex contextual cues, are particularly effective at detecting semantic spam. Furthermore, our analysis indicated that both search engine-based and list-based training result in the development of spam detectors that are capable of learning the underlying grammar and vocabulary associated with semantic spam, thereby establishing a basis for future research into the application of contextualized language frameworks to other search engine optimization techniques. A long-standing hypothesis in neurogenesis suggests that the varied distances that cells migrate from the ventricular zone to the cortical plate are responsible for the complex patterns seen in brain map formation. Studying the zebrafish retina, we find that this idea is incorrect for at least one type of cell: intermediate progenitor cells. Instead of relying on this 'distance-code' hypothesis, we discover that cell position is determined during a different stage of development. By examining and modeling the displacement of these cells as they move between the ventricular zone and the retina's outer layers, we find that a random dispersal process accounts for their final positions. Our research provides a new understanding of cell migration and offers a framework for studying other cellular movements within developing tissues. Furthermore, it suggests that the retina's spatial mapping process involves multiple distinct stages, each with its own unique mechanisms. Overall, our findings provide valuable insights for researchers seeking to uncover the underlying processes that generate the intricate patterns found in brain structures formed through cell migration. In the case of the zebrafish retina, we reveal that cellular dispersion is crucial for the pattern's formation. Furthermore, our discovery that the retina's cell distribution pattern does not require a feedback loop from the retina to the spinal cord challenges previous assumptions in the field. In fact, our data suggests that this loop, if present, has a minimal effect on the pattern. On the other hand, we find that the retina's cell distribution pattern is influenced by a short-range attraction between cells when they are in the ventricular zone. This interaction plays a vital role in preparing the retina for the dispersal of cells that will ultimately occupy its most distant layers. Our research provides a new understanding of the processes that shape the retina's cellular structure and raises questions about the processes that govern the mapping of brain structures formed through cellular dispersion. Studying the retina's cell distribution pattern has also implications for our understanding of the development of other tissues and the potential links between these processes. Research cooperation networks are built around individuals working together on specific research projects, their collaboration history, and current circumstances. These networks have been utilized in various settings to achieve a variety of objectives by analyzing node attributes and network structure. However, the inherent transient nature of academic cooperation networks poses significant challenges to existing methods used to analyze them. Current approaches often focus on static properties without considering the underlying dynamics that drive changes within the network. In contrast, this research aims to address this limitation by incorporating temporal elements into the analysis of cooperation networks. In order to achieve this, a set of temporal-based metrics has been proposed to explore the underlying mechanisms that influence the lifespan of research collaborations. These metrics were then applied to a dataset of paper co-authorships from the field of computer science. The results showed that many nodes in these networks have characteristics of both temporal stability and change, and that there are different groups of nodes that have varying durations of collaboration. Additionally, some nodes only engage in short-term collaborations, while others participate in projects that last for many years. Furthermore, various conditions that can either prolong or shorten the lifespan of collaborations have been identified. These conditions include both temporal attributes of the involved researchers and the average duration of their collaborations, with specific conditions that can lead to either short or long-term collaborations. The findings of this study can help create policies and programs that provide effective support to researchers in order to maintain the health of the scientific system as a whole. The proposed temporal-based metrics and modeling techniques can also be applied to other types of dynamic networks that are involved in the pursuit of innovative goals. In conclusion, analyzing cooperation networks using time-based methods can lead to a more comprehensive understanding of these networks and the temporary associations that they are based on, which can further enable the discovery of new patterns and laws governing their behavior. The Aberdeen Tunnel facility, situated in Scotland, offers a suitable environment for studying spallation neutrons through the collision of 800 MeV protons with a 10 meter-long graphite target. However, the facility's extensive size and the scattered nature of the neutron production make it challenging to determine the underlying processes that occur when these neutrons interact with matter. In this context, a device has been designed for use in the Aberdeen Tunnel facility, with the aim of detecting and analyzing spallation neutrons as they emerge from the end of the tunnel and travel through an air-filled tunnel segment spanning 7 meters in length. The devicecomprises of six 1-meter-long sections, each containing 32 scintillator neutron detection modules that can identify both the location and depth of interacting neutrons along with the time of the interaction. When combined, this information allows for the calculation of a neutron's time-of-flight as it travels through the tunnel, taking into account any discrepancies in its actual path. This device will provide valuable data for the development of more accurate models predicting neutron behavior in streaming scenarios. We describe the objectives of the TESS-Keck Survey in detail, focusing on assessing the sensitivity of transit light curve reconstruction and verifying predictions related to the TESS mission. Additionally, we outline the target selection for the survey, which includes a diverse range of asteroids, planets, and other key objects orbiting 343 different stars. These targets were chosen to represent various conditions, including various stellar types, different planetary architectures, and various orbiting bodies across the sky. The survey will utilize the Keck/NIRES to take high-resolution spectral images of 507 candidate transiting systems, including 434 from the TESS mission, and will significantly impact future studies by providing comprehensive analysis of these systems. The resulting data will include measurements of stellar mass, radius, density, surface gravity, temperature, metallicity, and [α/Fe]. Furthermore, the survey will provide accurate measurements of the radii, masses, densities, surface gravities, temperatures, and orbital periods of the orbiting bodies, as well as analyses of the planetary systems' architecture and the host stars' global characteristics. The survey's results will also contribute to the development of the TESS follow-up strategy. The survey's data and analysis will be publicly available to support future studies. The survey is being conducted in partnership with the TESS Follow-up Observing Program, the Ground-Based Observing Program, the NASA Keck Observatory, and the MIT Institute for Astrophysical Research. The initial phase of the survey began in October 2018 and data collection is ongoing. The survey's results will be presented in a series of scientific papers to be published in the Astronomical Journal. The survey's target list is available on the TESS Follow-up Observing Program's website.
